**Artificial intelligence (AI)** is a broad name for computer systems that do tasks we normally link with human thinking: recognising speech, sorting information, translating, predicting and writing. You have probably used AI for years without calling it that. The spam filter in Gmail, the word suggestions on your phone keyboard, the fastest-route advice in Google Maps and the face unlock on many phones are all AI.

Since late 2022 a newer kind has become popular: **generative AI**. Instead of only sorting or predicting, it produces new text, images, audio or video when you type a request. The best known are chatbots such as **ChatGPT** (OpenAI), **Gemini** (Google), **Claude** (Anthropic), **Microsoft Copilot** and **Meta AI**, which appears inside WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook in some countries.

This course is mainly about generative AI, because that is what most people now use directly. But the same lesson applies to both: AI learns from patterns in data. It does not understand the world the way a person does, and it does not know when it is wrong unless it has been built to check.
What chatbots are genuinely good at
**First drafts**: letters, reports, lesson notes, meeting agendas, job descriptions.
**Rewriting**: making text shorter, simpler, more formal or friendlier.
**Summarising** a long document you paste in, so you know where to read closely.
**Explaining** a concept in simple words, then again with an example.
**Brainstorming**: twenty ideas for a workshop title, of which you keep three.
**Structuring**: turning messy notes into a table, checklist or outline.
Where they often fail
**Facts, figures and recent events**: they can invent names, dates, laws, prices and quotes. This is called a **hallucination**.
**Sources**: they may cite books, articles or web links that do not exist.
**Arithmetic** in long calculations, especially when numbers are written inside sentences.
**Local detail**: Nigerian procedures, fees, place names and languages such as Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo and Pidgin are often handled less accurately than English or American topics.
**Judgement about people**: decisions on hiring, health, credit or discipline need a responsible human, not a chatbot.
Confident is not correct
A chatbot writes a wrong answer in the same calm, fluent tone as a right one. Fluency is what it is built for. Accuracy is something you must check.
A simple test before you use AI

Ask two questions about any task. First: **how reliable is AI for this kind of task?** Drafting and rewriting are high; precise facts and local rules are low. Second: **how much harm would a mistake cause?** A wrong word in a birthday message is low harm. A wrong dosage, fee, legal deadline or bank detail is high harm. Put the two answers together and you know how to proceed.

How a chatbot builds an answer: tokens, training and hallucinations
Describe in plain words how a large language model produces text
Use key terms correctly: prompt, token, context window, training data, knowledge cutoff

Chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude run on a **large language model**, usually shortened to **LLM**. An LLM is a very large computer program that has been trained on a huge amount of text from books, websites and other sources. During training it learned one main skill: given some text, **predict what comes next**.

When you type a question, the model does not look up a stored answer. It reads your words and predicts the next small piece of text, adds it, then predicts the next piece, and so on, until the answer is complete. This is why answers appear on screen word by word. It is also why the model can produce a sentence that sounds right but is false: it is choosing likely words, not checking facts.

Counting tokens

OpenAI's own guidance gives a rule of thumb for English: **one token is about 4 characters**, and **100 tokens is about 75 words**. Other languages, including Yoruba, Hausa and Igbo with their tone marks, usually need more tokens for the same meaning. Tokens matter because free plans and context windows have limits, and paid developer tools charge by the token.
Worked example: will my report fit?
For example, Zainab wants a chatbot to summarise a 3,000-word project report for her NGO. She wants to know roughly how many tokens it will use.
Rule: 100 tokens is about 75 words, so 1 word is about 100 / 75 = 1.33 tokens.
Report: 3,000 words x 1.33 = about 4,000 tokens.
Her instruction prompt is about 60 words, so 60 x 1.33 = about 80 tokens.
She asks for a 300-word summary: 300 x 1.33 = about 400 tokens.
Total for the exchange: 4,000 + 80 + 400 = about 4,480 tokens.

About 4,500 tokens is well inside the context window of the main chatbots today, so the whole report fits. A 300-page book would not fit in many free plans, and she would need to work chapter by chapter.
Why hallucinations happen

A model fills gaps with plausible text. If you ask for "three studies on market women in Kano" and its training data has little on that topic, it may still produce three neat titles with authors and years, because that is what such an answer usually looks like. The titles can be entirely invented. The same happens with phone numbers, fees, section numbers of laws and quotations from famous people.
**Gaps in training data**: less text about a topic means more guessing. Local Nigerian topics are often thin.
**Knowledge cutoff**: anything that changed after training, such as a new fee or policy, is unknown to the model.
**Pressure to answer**: models are trained to be helpful, so they tend to give an answer rather than say "I don't know".
**Long chats**: in very long conversations, early details can be lost or mixed up.
What reduces hallucinations
Give the source yourself: paste the document and say "answer only from the text below".
Ask the model to say "not stated in the text" if the answer is missing.
Use a tool with web search for current facts, then open and read the links it shows.
Ask for exact quotes from your pasted text so you can find them and confirm.
Keep chats focused; start a new chat for a new task.
Ask it to show where
When a chatbot summarises your document, ask: "For each point, quote the sentence it came from." If it cannot quote it, treat the point as unreliable.

The language gap

Most chatbots learned mainly from English text on the internet. Far less written material exists online in Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo, Pidgin and hundreds of other African languages. The result: translations and answers in these languages can be stiff, wrong in tone marks, or simply mistaken. Groups such as **Masakhane**, a grassroots research community for African language technology, work to close this gap, but you should still have a fluent speaker check anything important before it goes to members.
Check translations before sharing
If you use AI to translate a health notice, savings rule or meeting decision into Hausa or Igbo, ask a fluent speaker to read it before you send it. A wrong word can change the meaning completely.
Where AI is genuinely useful here
**Office and programme work**: drafting reports, minutes, letters and training handouts.
**Learning**: explaining a hard topic in simple words, making practice questions, planning study time.
**Small business**: product descriptions, customer replies, simple price lists, ideas for stock displays.
**Community leadership**: turning long notes into clear announcements, preparing agendas and checklists.
**Accessibility**: reading text aloud, turning voice notes into text, making large-print versions.

Worked example: is it worth it?
For example, Hadiza is a programme officer in Kaduna who writes four field reports a month, as in the comparison above.
Time per report without AI: 30 + 90 + 20 = 140 minutes.
Time per report with AI: 30 + 25 + 35 = 90 minutes.
Saving per report: 140 - 90 = 50 minutes.
Saving per month: 50 x 4 = 200 minutes, which is 3 hours 20 minutes.
Saving per year: 200 x 12 = 2,400 minutes, which is 40 hours.
Hadiza gains about 40 working hours a year, roughly five full working days, from one task, while still checking every fact. That is a real, honest case for AI, not a hopeful guess.

Notice what made the saving trustworthy: she measured her own times, included checking, and kept a human responsible for the final report. When you later advise a team or client, use the same method instead of quoting general promises about AI.
Data and cost on a phone
Typing text to a chatbot uses little mobile data compared with voice chat, image creation or video. If data is costly, prefer typed prompts, and download long reports on Wi-Fi.
Questions to ask about any new AI app

New apps often advertise themselves as "AI made for Africa" or promise to answer any question in your language. Some are excellent; some are copies built to collect data. Before you or your members rely on one, ask:
Who made it? Is there a real company name, website and contact address?
Is it in the official Google Play Store or Apple App Store, with a privacy policy you can read?
Where does your data go, and can you delete your account and chats?
Does it ask for permissions it does not need, such as your contacts or SMS?
Does it ask for payment or bank details before you have even tried it?
If you cannot answer these questions clearly, use one of the well-known tools from Lesson 2.1 instead.

Removing personal details before you paste

Often you need AI help with a document that contains personal data. The safe habit is to **anonymise** it first: replace names with roles or letters, remove phone numbers and addresses, and round exact amounts if they are not needed.
Worked example: anonymising a complaint before asking for help
For example, Blessing manages a small savings group in Ibadan. A member has sent a long, angry voice note that Blessing has typed up. She wants AI help to write a calm reply.
Original line: "Mrs Funmilayo Adeyemi, 0803 000 0000, of 12 Oke-Ado Road, says her 45,000 naira contribution was not recorded."
She replaces the name with "Member A", deletes the phone number and address, and keeps the amount because it matters to the reply.
Anonymised line: "Member A says her 45,000 naira contribution was not recorded."
She opens a Temporary Chat and asks: "Write a calm, respectful reply to a savings group member who says her contribution was not recorded. We are checking the records and will respond within 3 days."
She pastes the draft into WhatsApp, adds the member's name herself, and checks the 3-day promise is realistic before sending.
The chatbot never sees the member's name, phone number or address, yet Blessing still gets a good draft in two minutes.
AI voice and video scams

Criminals now use AI to copy voices and faces. If a call or voice note from a "relative" or "boss" asks for urgent money or codes, hang up and call them back on the number you already have, or ask a question only the real person would know.

Most disappointing AI results come from vague prompts. "Write a report" gives the model almost nothing, so it fills the gaps with generic text. A good prompt gives it the same information you would give a new assistant on her first day.

A clear prompt turns a generic draft into one that fits your real task.
Five parts of a clear prompt
Part
Question it answers
Example
Role
Who should the AI act as?
"Act as an experienced adult literacy trainer."
Task
What exactly should it produce?
"Write a one-page handout explaining how to read a bank statement."

"For women traders in Jos who use a phone banking app but find statements confusing."

Compare the difference. A weak prompt says: "Write a handout on bank statements." The result is usually a long, generic page aimed at nobody in particular, with words like "reconciliation" left unexplained. The strong prompt in the table above tells the model who the readers are, what they already know, how long it should be and what to avoid, so the first draft is already close to usable and needs only checking and small edits.
You do not need all five every time, but the more the task matters, the more parts you should include. Writing the prompt in your phone notes first, then pasting it, helps you think it through.
The workflow
Prompt, draft, check, edit
Define the task
Prompt with context
Review the draft
Check facts and numbers
Edit and own it
If the review shows big problems, go round again with a better prompt rather than patching a weak draft.
**Define**: write one sentence on what the finished work must achieve and who will use it.
**Prompt**: use the five parts, and paste any source text the answer should be based on.
**Review**: read the whole draft. Does it answer the task? Is the tone right for the audience?
**Check**: verify every name, date, number and claim (Lesson 2.3 shows how).
**Edit and own**: rewrite in your voice, add what only you know, and remove anything you cannot confirm.
Improving a weak answer
The first answer is a starting point. Instead of starting again, tell the model exactly what to change. Useful follow-ups:
"Make it simpler: short sentences, no jargon, as if for someone who left school after primary."
"Cut it to half the length and keep the steps."
"Give me three different openings so I can choose."
"What questions should I answer to make this more accurate for my situation?"
"List any facts in your answer that I should check before using it."
Worked example: a meeting summary from rough notes
For example, Ruth is secretary of a women's association in Calabar. After a 2-hour meeting she has 400 words of rough notes and must send minutes to 35 members by evening.
Define: "Clear minutes that record decisions, who will act, and deadlines, readable on WhatsApp."

Prompt: "Act as an experienced association secretary. Turn the notes below into minutes for 35 members. Format: date, attendance, 4 to 6 decisions as numbered points, an action table with person and deadline. Use only what is in the notes; write NOT STATED where something is missing. Under 300 words." She pastes the notes with members' surnames replaced by initials.
Review: the draft is clear but lists a deadline of "30 June" for the hall booking. Her notes said "end of the month".
Check: she asks the treasurer and confirms the real deadline is 28 June, then corrects it. She also sees the AI wrote attendance as 30; her notes say 27, so she fixes it.
Edit: she puts back members' full names, adds a line thanking the hosts, and sends.
Ruth finishes in about 25 minutes instead of over an hour, and two errors the AI introduced (a guessed date and a wrong attendance figure) were caught because she checked against her notes.
Use NOT STATED
Telling the model to write NOT STATED, or similar, when information is missing makes it far less likely to fill gaps with guesses, and shows you exactly what to find out.
When to stop prompting

If three rounds of follow-ups have not fixed the draft, the problem is usually that the model lacks information only you have. Stop, write that section yourself, and use AI only for tidying. Also stop when the task is personal: a condolence message or an apology to a colleague should sound like you, not a template.
Say when AI helped

In many workplaces and schools it is now expected that you say when AI helped produce work. A simple line such as "Drafted with AI assistance and checked by Ruth O." builds trust. Follow your organisation's rules.
This workflow works for letters, handouts, lesson plans, proposals and reports alike. The quality comes from your definition, your context and your checking, not from any secret prompt.

Checking is the skill that separates an AI-literate professional from a casual user. Anyone can get a fluent answer. Your value is knowing which parts to trust and proving the rest.
A person checking data against a list
Every fact, figure and source in AI output needs checking before it is shared.
What to check, in order
**Numbers**: totals, percentages, dates, prices, quantities.
**Names and titles**: people, organisations, laws, agencies, books.
**Sources and links**: does the reference exist, and does it say what the AI claims?
**Instructions**: steps on official processes, such as registering a business or applying for a grant.
**Tone and fairness**: does it stereotype any group of people?
The SIFT method for facts
SIFT is a fact-checking method developed by digital literacy educator Mike Caulfield. It was designed for web content and works well for AI answers.
SIFT: four moves
Stop
Investigate the source
Find better coverage
Trace to the original
Pause before trusting a claim, then confirm it from reliable, original sources.
Move
What you do with an AI claim
Notice a specific claim (a fee, a date, a statistic) and do not share it yet
If the AI gave a link, open it. Is it a real, official or reputable site?
Search the claim yourself and see what official or trusted sources say
Go to the first source: the agency's website, the law itself, the original report
Worked example: correcting an AI answer with wrong figures

For example, Ifeoma runs a tailoring business in Onitsha. She asked a chatbot to work out her profit margin and it replied: "You sold 40 gowns at 18,000 naira each and spent 450,000 naira on materials and labour, so your profit is 270,000 naira, a margin of 60%."
Stop: two numbers to check, the profit and the margin.
Revenue: 40 x 18,000 = 720,000 naira.
Profit: 720,000 - 450,000 = 270,000 naira. The AI is right here.
Margin: profit divided by revenue, 270,000 / 720,000 = 0.375, which is 37.5%.
The AI's 60% is wrong. It divided profit by costs (270,000 / 450,000 = 0.6), which is a different measure called markup on cost.
She records the error and the correct figure in her check record.
Profit is 270,000 naira and the profit margin is 37.5%, not 60%. Had she used the AI figure, she might have cut prices thinking she had more room than she does.
Use a calculator, not the chatbot
For any sum that matters, redo it on your phone calculator or in a spreadsheet. Ask the AI to show each step so you can see exactly where it went wrong.
Checking sources

If a chatbot cites a book, article or law, search for the exact title. Common problems: the title does not exist; it exists but by a different author; or it exists but does not say what the AI claimed. For Nigerian processes, trace to the official site, for example cac.gov.ng for business registration, ndpc.gov.ng for data protection, or nafdac.gov.ng for product registration.
Checking images and screenshots

AI can now produce realistic photos, flyers and screenshots. Before you forward a striking image or a "screenshot" of an announcement, look closely: hands with odd fingers, writing that turns into nonsense, logos slightly wrong, or lighting that does not match. Use **Google Lens** (search with an image) to see where else the picture has appeared and when. For announcements about grants, jobs or payments, go to the organisation's official website or verified social media page. If you cannot confirm it, do not share it, even with a warning.
Bias and stereotypes

Because AI learns from human data, it can repeat human bias. Image tools asked for "a CEO" may show mostly men; text tools may assume a nurse is a woman and an engineer is a man, or describe African countries mainly through poverty. Research by Joy Buolamwini and others has shown that some face analysis systems performed worse on darker-skinned women than on lighter-skinned men.
Read AI text and ask: would this sound fair if it described my own community?
When generating images of people, state who you want to see, for example "a Nigerian woman engineer at work".
Never use AI alone to rank, select or reject people for jobs, loans, admissions or support.

Recognise when AI is not the answer

When a school, NGO or small business asks "How can we use AI?", the wrong response is to start with tools. The right response is to start with their work. **Discovery** means understanding what people actually do each week, what slows them down, and what would go wrong if a mistake slipped through.
A person surrounded by question marks
Good AI advice starts with questions about the work, not with a list of tools.
Discovery questions
Ask these in a short meeting or by voice note, and write the answers down in their words.
Which written or repeated tasks take the most time each week?
Who reads the result, and what happens if it contains a mistake?
Does the task involve personal data about members, students, patients or clients?
Are staff already using AI tools? Which ones, and for what?
What devices and data budget do staff have?
Are there rules from funders, regulators or the board about data or AI?
What would success look like in three months?
Ask about current use
In many organisations some staff already use chatbots quietly, sometimes with sensitive data. Asking openly, without blame, gives you the real starting point.
Running the discovery meeting
Agree the time and who will attend: ideally the leader plus two or three people who do the daily work.
Explain the purpose in one sentence: "I want to understand your work so any AI advice fits you."
Ask the questions one at a time and let people give examples. Ask "Can you show me?" when they mention a document.
Write down tasks exactly as people describe them, with how often they happen and how long they take.
Close by reading back the main tasks and asking: "Did I miss anything important?"
Send a short thank-you message and say when they will receive your summary.
Listen more than you speak. Staff who do the work often know exactly where time is wasted, and they are the people who will have to use, or resist, whatever you recommend.
Build a task inventory

List every task mentioned, then score each on two scales from 1 to 5. **Value**: how much time AI could save, or how much quality it could add (5 is most). **Risk**: how much harm a mistake or data leak would cause (5 is most). Then plot each task.

Discovery often reveals problems AI cannot fix. If reports take long because nobody has the data, the fix is a better record-keeping habit. If staff miss deadlines because of unclear roles, the fix is management. Saying "AI will not help here, but this will" builds more trust than selling a tool.

Once you can use AI critically, others will ask for help: a cooperative wanting a training day, an NGO wanting staff guidance, a school wanting a policy. Whether you do this as paid work or as a volunteer, you need a clear cost, a clear proposal and clear limits.
A person reviewing a contract document
A written proposal with clear limits protects both you and the group you serve.
Cost before you price
List every cost, including your time. Then decide your price or, if volunteering, what support you need to cover expenses.
Worked example: costing a one-day workshop

For example, Folake is asked by a market women's association in Abeokuta to run a one-day "Using AI safely on your phone" workshop for 20 members. All figures are approximate and for illustration; use your own local prices.
Preparation: 6 hours. Delivery: 6 hours. Follow-up support on WhatsApp: 2 hours. Total time: 14 hours.
She values her time at 5,000 naira an hour (her choice): 14 x 5,000 = 70,000 naira.
Printing a 4-page handout for 20 people at about 100 naira a page: 20 x 4 x 100 = 8,000 naira.
Transport there and back: about 6,000 naira.
Data for demonstrations: about 3,000 naira.
Direct costs: 8,000 + 6,000 + 3,000 = 17,000 naira. Total cost including time: 70,000 + 17,000 = 87,000 naira.
Cost per participant: 87,000 / 20 = 4,350 naira.
Folake quotes 90,000 naira for the day (about 4,500 naira per member), which covers her costs. If the association cannot pay, she knows exactly what support to ask a sponsor for.

Honest expectations

Do not promise that AI will "double productivity" or "replace staff". You cannot verify such claims for a specific group. Report these numbers honestly in a short follow-up message, including what did not go well and what you will change next time.

Teams that use AI without agreed rules end up with uneven quality, leaked data and confusion about who is responsible. A short, clear **AI use policy** solves this. It does not need lawyers' language. It needs plain rules people can follow on their phones.
A team working together around a shared board
A short shared policy lets a whole team use AI the same safe way.
Seven parts of a one-page policy
Example wording
"We use AI to save time on drafting and summarising, while protecting the people we serve."
Approved tools
"Staff may use the free versions of ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot from the official apps."
Allowed uses
"First drafts, rewriting, summaries of non-confidential documents, idea lists, training materials."
Not allowed
"Decisions about hiring, discipline, admissions or support; medical or legal advice; creating images or audio of real people without consent."
Data rules
"No names, phone numbers, ID numbers, bank details or health information of members or clients. Anonymise first."
Human review
"A named person checks every fact and figure before anything is sent outside the team."
Disclosure and review
"We say when AI helped with published work. This policy is reviewed every six months."

Base your rules on recognised principles: UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI stresses human oversight, fairness, transparency and privacy; the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sets the legal baseline for personal data. Where your organisation has funders or regulators, check their rules too.
Deepfakes and consent

Never create or share AI images, video or voice of a real person without their clear permission, and never use AI to make anyone appear to say or do something they did not. This can cause serious harm and may break the law.
When the policy is broken
Sooner or later someone will paste personal data into a chatbot or send out an AI error. Respond calmly and quickly, because the aim is to limit harm and learn, not to shame.
Find out exactly what happened: which tool, what data or error, and who received it.
Limit the harm: delete the chat, correct the message, and tell anyone who received wrong information.
If other people's personal data was exposed, tell the person responsible for data protection in your organisation, who will judge whether the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 requires further steps.
Agree what will prevent a repeat, such as a reminder session or a clearer rule.
Record the incident and the fix, and use it at the next policy review.

You have used AI for years. The spam filter in Gmail, your keyboard's word suggestions and face unlock are all AI.
Since late 2022, generative AI has become popular. It produces new text, images or audio when you type a request.
Today you will learn how a chatbot builds its answer, and why it sometimes makes things up.
And you will learn a simple test for where AI can safely help you.
Two families
Predictive AI and generative AI
Sorts, scores or forecasts
Spam filter
Fraud alert from your bank
Traffic estimate on a map
Makes new content from a prompt
A chatbot drafting a letter
Photo turned into a cartoon
An AI voice reading text aloud
Predictive AI learns patterns from past data to sort, score or forecast, like your bank's fraud alert.
Generative AI produces new content in answer to a request, called a prompt. Neither kind understands the world the way a person does.
Inside the chatbot
How a chatbot builds an answer
It chooses likely words. It does not check facts.
Your text is split into tokens
The model predicts the next token
It adds that token and repeats
The answer appears on your screen
Chatbots run on a large language model, or LLM, trained to predict what comes next.
Step 1. You type a prompt.
Step 2. Your words are split into tokens, small pieces of text. One English token is about 4 characters.
Step 3. The model predicts the next token.
Step 4. It adds it and repeats, again and again. That is why answers appear word by word.
Step 5. You see the answer. Nothing in that loop checks it against reality. The model chooses likely words. It does not check facts.
Hallucinations
Why chatbots make things up
Less text on a topic means more guessing. Local Nigerian topics are often thin.
Anything that changed after training, like a new fee or policy, is unknown to the model.
Models are trained to be helpful, so they give an answer instead of saying I don't know.
A confident answer that is false is called a hallucination, like a fake law or a book that does not exist.
The first cause is gaps in training data. Where there is little text, the model guesses.
The second is the knowledge cutoff, the date after which the model learned nothing new.
The third is pressure to answer. And a wrong answer sounds just as calm and fluent as a right one.
Cut the errors
Paste the source: answer only from this text
Ask it to say not stated in the text
Use web search, then open the links
Ask for exact quotes you can find
Start a new chat for a new task
The best protection is to give the source yourself. Paste your document and say, answer only from the text below.
Tell it to say not stated in the text if the answer is missing.
For current facts, use web search, then open the links it shows.
Ask it to quote where each point came from. No quote means unreliable.
And start a new chat for a new task.
Before you use AI
The reliability and risk test
Match the amount of checking to the harm a mistake could cause.
How reliable is AI for this task?
How much harm would a mistake cause?
High reliability, low harm: use, light check
Medium harm: use it, then check every fact
Low reliability, high harm: go to the source
Before you use AI, ask two questions. First, how reliable is AI for this task? Drafting is high. Precise facts and local rules are low.
Second, how much harm would a mistake cause? A wrong fee, dosage, legal deadline or bank detail is high harm.
High reliability and low harm: use it freely with a light check.
Higher harm: use it, then check every fact.
Low reliability and high harm: avoid AI and go to the official source or a qualified person. Health, money and legal matters need that care.

You do not need a laptop or a paid plan. Free versions of ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude or Copilot run on your phone.

Day one
Official app or website only
Long unique password, two-step on
Training on your chats switched off
Finish these five checks before you use any AI tool for real work.
Download only from the Google Play Store or Apple App Store, from the real developer. Fake AI apps are a common way to steal data and money.
Use a long, unique password and turn on two-step verification.
In settings, switch off training on your chats where the tool allows it. In ChatGPT, that is under Data Controls. Use Temporary Chat for sensitive work.
And never paste ID, bank or client data.

Never paste BVN, NIN, bank or card numbers, passwords or one-time codes. Never paste other people's phone numbers, addresses or health details without permission.
Under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, you are responsible for other people's personal data.
For example, Blessing runs a savings group in Ibadan. Before asking for help with a complaint, she changes the member's name to Member A and deletes the phone number and address.

Clear prompts
Role: who should the AI act as?
Task: what exactly should it produce?
Context: who is it for?
Format: what shape should it take?
Limits: what must it avoid or include?
Vague prompts give generic answers. Give the AI what you would give a new assistant on her first day. First, a role, like an experienced adult literacy trainer.
Second, the task. For example, a one-page handout on reading a bank statement.
Third, context. Women traders in Jos who use a phone banking app but find statements confusing.
Fourth, format. A short intro, 5 numbered steps and a 3-question self-check.
Fifth, limits. Simple English, under 350 words, no invented bank names or fees.
Define, prompt, review, check, edit
Write NOT STATED where something is missing. No guessing.
Define what done looks like
Prompt with the five parts
Review the whole draft
Check every name, date and number
Edit it into your voice and own it
Step 1. Write one sentence on what the finished work must achieve, and who will use it.
Step 2. Prompt with the five parts, and paste any source text the answer should come from.
Step 3. Review the whole draft. Does it answer the task, in the right tone?
Step 4. Check every name, date and number.
Step 5. Edit it into your own voice, and remove anything you cannot confirm.
Tell the AI to write NOT STATED when information is missing. Then it is far less likely to guess.
If three rounds of follow-ups do not fix a draft, write that part yourself.
Checking facts
SIFT: four moves for any claim
If you cannot verify it, take it out.
Stop: do not share the claim yet
Investigate the source: open the link
Find better coverage: search it yourself
Trace to the original source
For facts, use SIFT, a method developed by Mike Caulfield. Stop. Notice a specific claim, like a fee or a date, and do not share it yet.
Investigate the source. If the AI gave a link, open it. Is it a real, official site?
Find better coverage. Search the claim yourself and see what trusted sources say.
Trace to the original. For business registration, that is cac.gov.ng. For product registration, nafdac.gov.ng.
If you cannot confirm a figure, name or reference, take it out or mark it unconfirmed.
Worked example
Ifeoma checks the AI's sums
For example, Ifeoma runs a tailoring business in Onitsha and sold 40 gowns at 18,000 naira each.
Margin: profit divided by revenue.
Revenue: 40 gowns x 18,000
Materials and labour
Profit
For example, Ifeoma asked a chatbot for her profit margin. It said her profit was 270,000 naira, a margin of 60%.
She redoes it on her phone calculator. 40 gowns at 18,000 naira is 720,000 naira.
Take away 450,000 naira for materials and labour, and the profit is 270,000 naira. The AI was right there.
But margin is profit divided by revenue. That gives 37.5%, not 60%. The AI divided by costs instead.
Had she trusted it, she might have cut her prices too far.

Discovery
Score every task for value and risk
Ask which tasks take the most time
Ask who reads it, and the harm of a mistake
Mark any task with personal data
Score value and risk from 1 to 5
Start with high value, low risk
Discovery means understanding what people actually do each week. Ask which written or repeated tasks take the most time.
Ask who reads the result, and what happens if it contains a mistake.
Mark every task that touches personal data. These need anonymisation rules and a named person accountable.
Then score each task from 1 to 5 for value, meaning time saved, and for risk, meaning harm if wrong.
High value and low risk tasks are the best first projects.
High-risk tasks stay with people, whatever their value.

Scope and payment
Agree it in writing
Your proposal
Purpose and deliverables
Exclusions: what you will not do
Timeline, price and payment
How success will be measured
Stay safe
Check new requests against it

Write a short proposal: purpose, deliverables, exclusions, responsibilities, timeline, price, and how success will be checked.
Promise skills you can measure, not claims that AI will double productivity.
When someone asks for more, like a Facebook page or a grant, check it against the proposal. If it is out of scope, offer a separate price.
Take payment by traceable transfer and confirm it in your account app. Screenshots of transfers can be faked.
Your AI policy
Purpose and approved tools
Allowed uses: drafts, summaries, ideas
Not allowed: decisions about people
Data rules: no names, IDs or health data
Human review, disclosure, review date
A one-page policy prevents leaked data and confusion. Start with its purpose, and which official apps are approved.
List the allowed uses, like first drafts, summaries and training materials.
List what is not allowed: decisions on hiring, discipline or admissions, and medical or legal advice.
Set data rules. No names, phone numbers, ID numbers, bank details or health information. Anonymise first.
Name a person who checks every fact before anything goes out. Say when AI helped, and review the policy every six months.
Safety
When things go wrong
Never create AI images, video or voice of a real person without clear permission.
Find out what happened. Delete the chat, correct the message, tell those who got it.
Tell your data protection lead, who checks what the Data Protection Act 2023 requires.
Never create or share AI images, video or voice of a real person without their clear permission. It can cause serious harm and may break the law.
If someone breaks the policy, respond calmly. The aim is to learn, not to shame. Find out what happened, correct it, and tell anyone who received wrong information.
If other people's personal data was exposed, tell the person responsible for data protection. Then record the incident and the fix.

Cost your time and every expense
Agree scope and payment in writing
A one-page policy keeps everyone safe
